steps.label: ImageNet is a database; ILSVRC is a competition · 1/3

narration.label: p0-b1.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: Use the nested regions to distinguish the database from the competition subset. ImageNet contains roughly fifteen million labeled images across about twenty-two thousand classes in the lecture’s description. ILSVRC selects a much smaller subset of about 1.2 million images and one thousand classes. These are approximate sizes. Images collected from the web receive human annotations; the competition and the full database are related, but they are not identical objects.

steps.label: ImageNet is a database; ILSVRC is a competition · 2/3

narration.label: p0-b2.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: The card on the right explains why a common benchmark matters. Using the same data and evaluation rule makes architecture comparisons more interpretable. It does not imply that all original photographs have the same dimensions. A model’s input size refers to what it receives after resizing or cropping. Always state that preprocessing separately instead of inferring an image size from the dataset name.

narration.label: p0-b3.mp3

Those are separate properties of the benchmark and its preprocessing.

steps.label: Top-5 asks whether the true class is among five guesses · 1/3

narration.label: p1-b1.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: Look at the ranked guesses for one image. The true label is cat, but the model ranks dog first, fox second, and cat third. These five entries are candidate classes for the same image, not five separate test examples. To evaluate the prediction, first hold the true label fixed, then apply the chosen rule to this ordered list of guesses.

steps.label: Top-5 asks whether the true class is among five guesses · 2/3

narration.label: p1-b2.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: The two lower cards apply different rules to the same ranking. Top-one is wrong because the highest-scoring class is dog. Top-five is correct because cat appears among the first five guesses. On a fixed collection of images, top-five error cannot exceed top-one error. A seventeen-percent top-five error on one thousand images means one hundred seventy true labels are absent from their respective top-five lists.

steps.label: Top-5 asks whether the true class is among five guesses · 3/3

narration.label: p1-b3.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: The conclusion interprets an error rate as a count of images failing the rule. If cat moves from third to fifth place, does top-five become wrong? No, it still includes the true label. If cat moves to sixth, top-five fails. Changing the metric changes the correctness criterion; it does not change the underlying ranking produced by the model.

narration.transcript: Female: The upper row shows five convolutional layers. Each kernel specification lists kernel count, height, width, and connected input channels. The first layer, for example, has ninety-six kernels of size eleven by eleven by three. Some later kernels connect to only half the preceding channels because of two-GPU grouping. Kernel depth must follow those actual connections, rather than automatically equal the total number of preceding feature maps.

steps.label: Two-GPU grouping explains reduced kernel depth · 1/3

narration.label: p3-b1.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: The two GPU panels explain the grouped layout. Each GPU had about three gigabytes of memory and received part of the feature maps. The labels forty-eight and one hundred ninety-two describe the channel depth seen by grouped paths. That is different from the number of output kernels. Splitting the network addressed both the capacity limit of a single device and the practical speed of training.

steps.label: Two-GPU grouping explains reduced kernel depth · 2/3

narration.label: p3-b2.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: The lower notes identify which layers are grouped. Layer two sees half the previous channels, and layers four and five also use grouped connections. Layer three sees the outputs from both GPUs, giving an input depth of two hundred fifty-six. To count convolution weights, multiply kernel area by the channels actually connected and the output-kernel count. Neither always halving depth nor always using every preceding channel is correct.

steps.label: Two-GPU grouping explains reduced kernel depth · 3/3

narration.label: p3-b3.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: The takeaway is to distinguish kernel count from kernel depth. If the previous layer has ninety-six maps but a group sees only half, what depth enters that group’s kernel count? Forty-eight channels. This does not mean there are forty-eight output kernels. One number describes connected inputs; the other describes how many output feature maps the layer produces.

steps.label: State input size and padding before following dimensions · 1/3

narration.label: p4-b1.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: Follow the side lengths from left to right. An input of two hundred twenty-seven becomes fifty-five after conv one and twenty-seven after pooling. Conv two preserves twenty-seven, the next pool gives thirteen, conv three through five preserve thirteen, and the final pool gives six. Every number refers to the side length of a square feature map within one consistent input-and-padding setup.

steps.label: State input size and padding before following dimensions · 2/3

narration.label: p4-b2.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: The formula says: add twice the padding to the input size, subtract kernel width, divide by stride, round down, and add one. Input two hundred twenty-four with no padding, kernel eleven, and stride four gives fifty-four, not fifty-five. Do not splice that result into the two-hundred-twenty-seven chain. Finally, six times six times two hundred fifty-six gives nine thousand two hundred sixteen flattened inputs for the classifier.

steps.label: State input size and padding before following dimensions · 3/3

narration.label: p4-b3.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: The bottom note keeps later fully connected counts consistent with the 227-based chain. Why does the unpadded 224 case give fifty-four? Subtract eleven, divide by four, round down to fifty-three, and add one. A small change at the input can affect every later dimension, so the input, padding, kernel, and stride must be specified together.

steps.label: Convolution uses compute; fully connected layers hold most weights · 1/3

narration.label: p5-b1.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: Compare the five convolutional layers in the upper part. Their weights depend on kernel area, actual connected input channels, and output-kernel count. A kernel is reused across spatial positions, so many output neurons do not imply a separate parameter set for every position. Together these convolutions have about 2.33 million weights. A large number of arithmetic operations and a large parameter store are different kinds of cost.

steps.label: Convolution uses compute; fully connected layers hold most weights · 2/3

narration.label: p5-b2.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: The bottom three fully connected layers dominate storage. The first alone has more than thirty-seven million weights; together the three have about 58.62 million, or 96.2 percent of the network’s weights. The bars share a linear scale with a zero baseline. This comparison establishes where the weights are stored, not where all computation necessarily occurs; convolution can still perform a great deal of repeated arithmetic.

steps.label: Convolution uses compute; fully connected layers hold most weights · 3/3

narration.label: p5-b3.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: The conclusion highlights weight sharing rather than neuron count. If a feature map doubles its number of spatial positions while keeping the kernel and channel counts fixed, do convolutional weights necessarily double? No: the same kernel weights are reused. The amount of computation can increase, which is precisely why parameter count and arithmetic cost should be reported separately.

steps.label: LRN suppresses a response when neighboring channels are strong · 1/3

narration.label: p6-b1.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: The top row fixes one spatial location and shows five neighboring channels. The center activation is one hundred and all four neighbors are zero. After local response normalization, the center output is about 43.9. The neighborhood runs across channels at that location; it is not a window over neighboring image positions. Keep that distinction in mind before comparing the second row.

steps.label: LRN suppresses a response when neighboring channels are strong · 2/3

narration.label: p6-b2.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: In the second row, the center remains one hundred, but every neighboring channel is also one hundred. The normalized center response falls to about 23.2. Nothing changed in its own original activation; the stronger neighbors increased the denominator. The comparison isolates cross-channel suppression. LRN is not batch normalization, which uses a different normalization rule and a different statistical context.

steps.label: LRN suppresses a response when neighboring channels are strong · 3/3

narration.label: p6-b3.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: The bottom statement summarizes the direction of the effect. If the center stays fixed and neighboring activations become stronger, does the normalized center increase or decrease in this example? It decreases because the denominator grows. The lesson is about the rule’s dependence on nearby channels, not a claim that all normalization methods perform the same operation.

steps.label: Clip the LRN window at channel boundaries · 1/3

narration.label: p7-b1.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: Read the fraction as the center activation divided by a normalization factor. Square the neighboring activations and sum them, multiply by alpha, add k, and raise that entire sum to the power beta. Here k is two, alpha is ten to the minus four, and beta is 0.75. The window contains at most five channels; near an edge, clip its indices between zero and the final valid channel.

Square the neighboring activations and sum them, multiply by alpha, add k, and raise that entire sum to the power beta. Here k is two, alpha is ten to the minus four, and beta is 0.75. The window contains at most five channels; near an edge, clip its indices between zero and the final valid channel.

steps.label: Clip the LRN window at channel boundaries · 2/3

narration.label: p7-b2.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: The lower pipeline places ReLU before LRN and maximum pooling after it in the first two convolutional stages. Pooling uses width three and stride two. If activations are tiny, the denominator is mainly two raised to 0.75, so the output is approximately 0.595 times the original activation. This limiting case is only an approximate fixed scaling, not a description of LRN for arbitrary activation strengths.

steps.label: Clip the LRN window at channel boundaries · 3/3

narration.label: p7-b3.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: The takeaway limits the tiny-activation approximation and distinguishes it from batch standardization. At the first channel, should the normalization window read nonexistent negative channel indices? No: truncate the window at the boundary. Consequently, the number of included channels can be smaller than five even though the nominal window size stays fixed.

steps.label: Windows overlap when width exceeds stride · 1/3

narration.label: p8-b1.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: The left diagram uses a window three cells wide whose starting position advances by two cells. Consecutive windows therefore share the middle cell. Overlap follows from window width and stride, independently of the values inside the cells. For a two-dimensional image, the same reasoning applies separately in the horizontal and vertical directions as the window moves over the feature map.

steps.label: Windows overlap when width exceeds stride · 2/3

narration.label: p8-b2.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: The right card locates pooling in AlexNet after convolutional layers one, two, and five. The first two pooling operations follow LRN. VGG instead uses window width two and stride two, so consecutive windows do not overlap. Pooling controls spatial sampling, while LRN normalizes across nearby channels; the presence of LRN does not determine whether the pooling windows overlap.

steps.label: Windows overlap when width exceeds stride · 3/3

narration.label: p8-b3.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: The conclusion returns to the geometric rule. If width and stride are both two, how many cells do adjacent windows share in this simple slice? None. With width three and stride two, they share one. Decide overlap from those two settings, rather than from the network name or whether another normalization operation happens nearby.

steps.label: Negative probability and negative log probability differ · 1/3

narration.label: p9-b1.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: The upper formula converts class scores to softmax probabilities by exponentiating each score and dividing by the sum of all exponentials. Standard classification loss is the negative logarithm of the probability assigned to the true class. The three-score example, two, one, and 0.1, produces probabilities about 0.659, 0.242, and 0.099. Their total is approximately one, allowing for rounding.

steps.label: Negative probability and negative log probability differ · 2/3

narration.label: p9-b2.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: Compare the two gradient cards when the true-class probability is only 0.01. For negative probability loss, first compute one minus that probability and multiply by the probability itself: the magnitude is 0.0099. For negative log probability, the magnitude is one minus the probability, or 0.99. Both encourage a larger true-class probability, but the correction signal is much stronger for the logarithmic loss when the model is badly wrong.

narration.label: p9-b3.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: The takeaway explains why omitting the logarithm changes optimization, even if the preferred direction seems unchanged. At true-class probability 0.01, are the two displayed gradient magnitudes equal? No: 0.99 is one hundred times 0.0099. These formulas concern the derivative with respect to the true-class score, under the stated softmax setup.
